Sporadic PPGLs The overall prevalence of recurrence in patients with sporadic phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) is approximately 14.7% and, looking specifically at sporadic PCC, the recurrence rate is only slightly lower at 14.2% ( 52 ). Disease recurrence (local and metastatic) for patients with sporadic PPGLs can occur after a prolonged disease-free period; roughly 65.8% are diagnosed within the first 5 years, but 29.1% are diagnosed at least 10 years after the initial tumour diagnosis, and 17.7% are diagnosed 15 years or more after the first diagnosis ( 53 ). The risk of recurrence is heavily influenced by specific clinical and biochemical features. Multivariable analyses have demonstrated that a noradrenergic/dopaminergic biochemical phenotype, a primary tumour diameter of >5 cm, and an extra-adrenal location are independent predictors of recurrent disease in sporadic cases. Younger age at initial diagnosis may also be a risk factor. Patients with small (<3 cm) sporadic adrenergic tumours have a notably low recurrence rate of just 3.2% ( 53 ).

Because recurrences can occur decades after the initial surgery, guidelines mandate extended follow-up tailored to the patient’s risk profile. Surveillance is recommended for at least 10 years in all patients operated on for a sporadic PPGL ( 13 , 52 ). However, because nearly 18% of recurrences happen beyond 15 years, extending follow-up past 15 years may be justified ( 53 ). For sporadic cases deemed high-risk (e.g. young age, large tumours ≥5 cm, extra-adrenal location, or noradrenaline dominance), lifelong annual follow-up is strongly recommended ( 53 ). The nature and intensity of the follow-up should be individualized based on the primary tumour’s characteristics. Patients with high-risk features require strict monitoring, whereas surveillance might not need to be as exhaustive for those with low-risk profiles, such as small adrenergic tumours. For functionally active tumours, annual measurement of plasma or urinary fractionated metanephrines (and optionally 3-methoxytyramine) is the standard method to screen for local or metastatic recurrences and new tumours and should be repeated 3 months after surgery and then at 6–12-month intervals depending on the patient’s clinical risk profile.

If the primary sporadic tumour did not secrete catecholamines, biochemical tests are inadequate for surveillance. These patients should undergo imaging tests (such as CT or MRI) every 1–2 years. In addition, an initial imaging test should be performed 3–6 months postoperatively ( 13 , 52 , 53 ) ( Table 3 ).

Predicting metastatic PPGL risk: existing and emerging diagnostic tools Clinical risk factors and histopathological and molecular markers Recent advances in predicting the metastatic potential of PPGLs highlight a paradigm shift towards integrating traditionally accepted clinical risk factors and histopathological features with multi-omic profiling, liquid biopsies, and artificial intelligence. As all PPGLs possess metastatic potential, identifying high-risk patients preoperatively and at initial diagnosis is a clinical priority to facilitate stratification of long-term follow-up.

Clinical risk factors for metastasis include extra-adrenal localization, large tumour size (particularly >5 cm), locally invasive tumours, and tumours arising in individuals with pathogenic germline SDHx variants, particularly in the SDHB gene. Histopathological features indicating a higher malignant risk include vascular or capsular invasion, high mitotic rate (>3/10 HPF), nuclear pleomorphism, and confluent necrosis. In a recent prospective study on tumour samples and liquid biopsies from 231 consecutive patients with PPGLs, the immunohistochemical loss of succinate dehydrogenase subunit B (SDHB) was a more powerful predictor of an SDHx status, while the prediction of metastasis and lower metastasis-free survival was achieved by a combination of 4 biomarker tools, namely telomerase maintenance, detection of circulating miR-483-5p, plasma succinate level, and SDHB immunohistochemistry ( 54 ). Overexpression of the mini-chromosome maintenance 6 (MCM6) protein, which is involved in DNA replication, has been associated with a higher incidence of distant organ metastasis and shows promise as a novel prognostic marker, though larger cohort studies are needed. In addition, tumours harbouring MAML3 fusion anomalies (detectable via nuclear overexpression) exhibit a distinctive, highly vascular tumour microenvironment and are linked to aggressive clinical behaviour ( 55 , 56 ).

While canonical TERT promoter point mutations are known drivers of metastasis, they are relatively rare in PPGLs. Recent whole-genome sequencing has revealed that somatic structural rearrangements (such as intra-chromosomal deletions and translocations) can modulate enhancers close to the TERT promoter, leading to abnormal activation of TERT in metastatic PPGLs. Hypermethylation of the TERT promoter is a highly accurate prognostic biomarker of metastatic PPGLs ( 39 , 57 ). Somatic pathogenic mutations in the ATRX gene are also significantly associated with metastatic progression and telomere dysregulation. Tumours with ATRX alterations consistently exhibit the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) phenotype, characterized by the presence of C-circles and longer telomeres ( 39 ). In metastatic patients treated with DNA alkylating chemotherapies (such as dacarbazine or temozolomide), multi-omic profiling has identified acquired resistance mechanisms, including MGMT overexpression and mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency leading to hypermutation (e.g. via MLH1 or MSH6 mutations) ( 39 ).

Metabolomic and liquid biopsy biomarkers Elevated plasma succinate (>4.94 μM) correlates with tumour burden and is highly effective at identifying patients carrying underlying SDHx mutations (which confer a high metastatic risk). It provides a rapid, non-invasive screening tool with 65% sensitivity and 92% specificity ( 54 ). This test is relatively inexpensive and offers a potentially affordable method to rapidly identify underlying pathogenic SDHx variants for individuals diagnosed in countries where genetic testing is not offered as current standard of care.

Liquid biopsies have identified miR-483-5p as the single best circulating microRNA classifier for metastatic status. Elevated levels of miR-483-5p correlate with tumour burden and predict the risk of developing future metastases ( 54 ). Finally, elevated plasma methoxytyramine indicates an undifferentiated, high-risk tumour phenotype with high specificity (85%); however, if interpreted in isolation, the sensitivity of plasma methoxytyramine is limited (52%) and as a biomarker for metastatic potential, it is best utilized alongside other clinical features ( 42 ).

Machine learning (ML) prediction models A significant advance in predictive accuracy has come from machine learning models that integrate diverse datasets and can complement or augment the judgement of human clinical specialists. A model utilizing nine routine features – plasma methoxytyramine, metanephrine, normetanephrine, age, sex, previous PPGL history, tumour location, tumour size, and multifocal disease – achieved a highly accurate prediction of metastasis (AUC of 0.942). Notably, this model achieved excellent diagnostic performance without requiring genetic data, making it highly practical for routine clinical use ( 42 ). Another multivariate model combined more advanced biological variables (circulating miR-483-5p, TERT promoter methylation, SDHB IHC, and plasma succinate) with standard clinical data (tumour size, age, site, germline status) and demonstrated diagnostic accuracy (AUC-ROC of 0.97) for predicting metastatic disease ( 54 ).

Summary This document provides an in-depth review of recent clinical advancements and international consensus guidelines regarding the diagnosis, treatment, and long-term management of PPGLs. The management of these rare neuroendocrine tumours is increasingly driven by specialized, multidisciplinary care. International collaborations fostered over the past decade have acted as the major catalyst for significant research advances and expert consensus guidelines in this field. Key findings from this article include the following: i) modern care of PPGLs is heavily driven by ‘genotype-first’ clinical management; ii) the importance of agreed specialized paediatric diagnostic and management protocols, acknowledging key differences in the biology of paediatric versus adult PPGLs; iii) systemic therapy is increasingly tailored based on the patient’s underlying genetic driver; and iv) the prediction of metastatic risk is evolving and improving with the integration of novel molecular biomarkers and machine learning models.

Summary A 37-year-old man with a long-standing history of daily cannabis use was evaluated for refractory hypertension and recurrent paroxysmal episodes of palpitations, diaphoresis, tremor, and anxiety. A consistent and striking clinical pattern had been observed over several years: symptoms reliably improved during active cannabis use and worsened within days of abstinence. This bidirectional relationship had guided prior evaluations towards anxiety disorder and cannabis withdrawal syndrome, and no biochemical endocrine workup had ever been performed. After a sustained period of abstinence precipitated more frequent and severe episodes, urinary fractionated metanephrines were measured and found to be markedly elevated: normetanephrine at 6,114 μg/24 h (reference range: ≤445; 13.7-fold) and total metanephrines at 11,662 μg/24 h (reference range: ≤757; 15.4-fold). Contrast-enhanced CT identified a 6.0 × 5.0 cm left adrenal mass with imaging characteristics consistent with phaeochromocytoma. Following preoperative alpha- and beta-adrenergic blockade, laparoscopic left adrenalectomy was performed without complications. Histopathology confirmed phaeochromocytoma with a PASS of 5. Symptoms resolved completely, and blood pressure normalised without antihypertensive therapy. We propose that chronic cannabis use may have partially attenuated the tumour’s catecholamine surges through a cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1)-mediated presynaptic mechanism, whereby delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) reduces acetylcholine release from cholinergic nerve terminals innervating the adrenal medulla, thereby attenuating chromaffin cell stimulation and catecholamine secretion. This hypothesis could explain the observed bidirectional symptom pattern and represents a biologically plausible, previously undescribed confounding interaction with important diagnostic implications. At 2-week postoperative follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and normotensive. At 3 months, he remained symptom-free without antihypertensive medication.

Learning points Chronic cannabis use may pharmacologically attenuate the clinical expression of phaeochromocytoma through a biologically plausible CB1 receptor-mediated presynaptic mechanism – whereby THC reduces acetylcholine release from cholinergic nerve terminals innervating the adrenal medulla, attenuating chromaffin cell stimulation and catecholamine secretion – potentially creating a presentation indistinguishable from anxiety disorder or cannabis withdrawal. This hypothesis is supported by the observed temporal pattern but requires further investigation to establish causality.

The pattern of symptom improvement during active cannabis use and exacerbation during abstinence, particularly when combined with refractory hypertension, may prompt biochemical evaluation for catecholamine excess rather than reinforcing a substance-related or psychiatric diagnosis. Cannabis withdrawal is associated with a significant rise in circulating epinephrine; in patients with a catecholamine-secreting tumour, withdrawal of the proposed CB1-mediated inhibitory tone could precipitate severe hyperadrenergic crises that are clinically indistinguishable from withdrawal without biochemical testing.

Measurement of plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines should not be deferred based on an apparently plausible psychiatric or substance-related explanation, particularly in patients with refractory hypertension and paroxysmal sympathomimetic symptoms.

While the classic triad of headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations in the setting of hypertension is well recognised, up to 20% of patients present with atypical features, including predominantly neuropsychiatric manifestations, such as anxiety, panic attacks, and autonomic instability ( 2 , 3 ). These presentations frequently lead to misdiagnosis as primary psychiatric disorders, with documented diagnostic delays ranging from months to more than a decade ( 3 ).

What has received no attention in the literature is the possibility that concurrent substance use could pharmacologically modulate the symptomatic expression of phaeochromocytoma. Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive constituent of cannabis, activates cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1) receptors. In the adrenal medulla, CB1 receptors are expressed presynaptically on cholinergic nerve terminals rather than directly on chromaffin cells; their activation by THC is thought to reduce acetylcholine release, thereby attenuating stimulation of chromaffin cells and catecholamine secretion ( 4 , 5 ). Although the precise mechanism in humans remains incompletely characterised, this pathway is biologically plausible and consistent with established adrenomedullary physiology. Separately, cannabis withdrawal is associated with a significant rise in circulating epinephrine, producing sympathomimetic symptoms, including sweating, tremor, and anxiety ( 6 ). In a patient harbouring an autonomously secreting adrenal tumour, this pharmacological dynamic could attenuate hyperadrenergic episodes during active use and amplify them during abstinence, creating a bidirectional clinical pattern that mimics anxiety or substance withdrawal at every evaluation.

We report a case in which this mechanism may have operated for several years, systematically delaying the diagnosis of a large left adrenal phaeochromocytoma. To our knowledge, this pharmacological confounding interaction has not been previously described in the context of phaeochromocytoma.

Case presentation A 37-year-old man with a history of daily cannabis use was referred for evaluation of refractory hypertension and recurrent paroxysmal episodes that had been occurring intermittently for several years. He reported smoking approximately two cannabis cigarettes daily since the age of 17 years, initially for recreational purposes and, in the six months preceding diagnosis, primarily to relieve recurrent episodes of anxiety, tinnitus, and transient visual disturbances. The episodes consisted of sudden-onset palpitations, profuse sweating, tremor, headache, and intense anxiety lasting minutes to hours. A clinically striking pattern had been observed consistently over that period: symptoms were noticeably less frequent and less severe during active cannabis use and returned with greater intensity within days of stopping, whether cessation was intentional or not. Periods of abstinence, typically lasting no longer than one week, were consistently associated with worsening symptoms, prompting resumption of cannabis use.

This temporal relationship had been interpreted by multiple prior providers as anxiety disorder with cannabis use disorder, or alternatively as cannabis withdrawal syndrome. Anxiety symptoms had been present for approximately three years, with marked worsening over the preceding six months, characterised by emotional lability and episodic euphoria. Anxiolytics and standard antihypertensive agents had produced no meaningful improvement. No biochemical endocrine evaluation had been performed at any prior contact.

After a sustained period of cannabis abstinence, the episodes became frequent and severe enough to prompt hospital evaluation. Four months before diagnosis, intermittent tinnitus and transient visual impairment developed, leading to evaluation for hypertensive emergencies. Despite treatment with telmisartan followed by amlodipine, blood pressure remained poorly controlled. One month before diagnosis, prazosin, amlodipine, and metoprolol were initiated while further evaluation was undertaken. During this period, the patient experienced episodes of transient loss of consciousness following hypertensive crises. Blood pressure was recorded at 195/110 mmHg during one of the paroxysms. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Given the constellation of paroxysmal hypertension, diaphoresis, and palpitations refractory to prior treatment, biochemical evaluation for phaeochromocytoma was initiated.

Investigation Twenty-four-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines were markedly elevated ( Table 2 ). Fractionated 24-h urinary metanephrines were selected as the initial biochemical test because they provide a reliable assessment of total catecholamine metabolite production over an extended period, which is particularly useful in patients with intermittent hormone secretion. Given the paroxysmal nature of this patient’s symptoms over several years, urinary metanephrines represented an appropriate diagnostic approach owing to their high specificity. Furthermore, urinary testing is less susceptible than plasma measurements to transient physiological fluctuations and pre-analytical variables, such as posture, stress, and sampling conditions – factors particularly relevant in a patient initially suspected of having anxiety ( 7 ). Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a well-defined, heterogeneous mass measuring 6.0 × 5.0 cm in the left adrenal gland, demonstrating heterogeneous enhancement without evidence of local invasion or distant metastatic disease, with imaging characteristics consistent with phaeochromocytoma ( Fig. 1 ).

Treatment The patient was started on phenoxybenzamine for alpha-adrenergic blockade. Once adequate alpha-blockade was established over approximately two weeks, a non-selective beta-blocker was added to the regimen. After three weeks of preoperative haemodynamic preparation, the patient underwent laparoscopic left adrenalectomy. The procedure was completed without intraoperative haemodynamic instability, with an estimated blood loss of approximately 200 mL ( Fig. 2 ).

Outcome and follow-up Histopathological examination of the resected specimen confirmed phaeochromocytoma. The tumour exhibited the characteristic zellballen architecture, with polygonal cells arranged in well-defined nests separated by sustentacular cells and a rich vasculature. Mitotic activity was low at 1 per 10 high-power fields, and no capsular or vascular invasion was identified. The tumour measured 6.2 cm and weighed 101 g on gross pathological examination, with a heterogeneous tan-yellow cut surface containing focal haemorrhagic areas. The Phaeochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score (PASS) was 5, placing the tumour in the intermediate-risk category ( Fig. 3 ). Immunohistochemical studies, Ki-67 proliferative index, and SDHB immunostaining were not performed as they were not part of the routine pathological evaluation at our institution. It should be noted that the PASS system demonstrates considerable interobserver variability and has limited ability to reliably predict malignant behaviour or metastatic potential when used in isolation; current recommendations advocate integrating clinical, biochemical, and pathological findings for postoperative risk stratification ( 8 ). The postoperative course was uneventful. Blood pressure normalised without antihypertensive medication. At 2-week postoperative follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, was normotensive, and demonstrated appropriate wound healing. At 3 months, he remained symptom-free without antihypertensive medication. Postoperative metanephrine measurements were not obtained owing to complete clinical resolution.

Given the patient’s relatively young age at presentation (37 years), genetic counselling and germline testing for hereditary phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma susceptibility syndromes would have been appropriate according to current recommendations. This represents a limitation of the present report, as an underlying hereditary predisposition cannot be excluded.

Discussion The most distinctive feature of this case is not the phaeochromocytoma itself, but the mechanism by which it remained may have remained undetected for years. The patient’s chronic cannabis use appears to have created a pharmacological environment in which catecholamine surges from the tumour were partially suppressed during active use, producing a clinical picture that fell within a range consistent with anxiety. When cannabis was discontinued, the proposed CB1-mediated inhibitory tone was removed, catecholamine release intensified, and the resulting symptom exacerbation was plausibly misread as withdrawal. This bidirectional pattern – improvement with use and exacerbation with abstinence – provided a compelling and internally consistent alternative explanation that discouraged further investigation at each clinical encounter.

The pharmacological basis for this hypothesis is grounded in established physiology. In the adrenal medulla, CB1 receptors are expressed presynaptically on cholinergic nerve terminals rather than directly on chromaffin cells. Activation of these receptors by THC is thought to reduce acetylcholine release, thereby attenuating the stimulation of chromaffin cells and their subsequent catecholamine secretion ( 4 , 5 ). Although the precise mechanism in humans remains incompletely characterised, this pathway is biologically plausible and consistent with known adrenomedullary neurotransmission. In parallel, chronic cannabis use is associated with blunted hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis reactivity and reduced sympathoadrenal responsiveness ( 9 ). During cannabis withdrawal, circulating epinephrine rises significantly, producing sympathomimetic symptoms, including sweating, tremor, and anxiety ( 6 ). In a patient with an autonomously secreting adrenal tumour, withdrawal of the proposed CB1-mediated inhibitory tone could predictably amplify the underlying catecholamine excess, which is exactly the temporal pattern this patient experienced, repeatedly, over several years.

This proposed mechanism is pharmacologically distinct from the nonspecific anxiolytic effect of cannabis. The hypothesised interaction operates at the adrenomedullary level, implying that the clinical masking may have been a direct consequence of CB1-mediated suppression of tumour catecholamine release rather than a sedative effect on symptom perception. This distinction has practical implications: cannabis use should not be assumed to explain paroxysmal sympathomimetic symptoms, particularly when accompanied by refractory hypertension. The co-occurrence of cannabis use with such symptoms should, if anything, heighten (not lower) the clinical index of suspicion for catecholamine excess.

Neuropsychiatric presentations of phaeochromocytoma, including anxiety, panic attacks, and autonomic instability, are well documented and frequently lead to extended diagnostic delays ( 3 , 10 ). The present case suggests a previously undescribed pharmacological dimension to this landscape. As cannabis use becomes increasingly prevalent worldwide, including among middle-aged adults at risk of PPGLs, clinicians should be aware that concurrent use may actively modify the symptomatic expression of a catecholamine-secreting tumour through the proposed adrenomedullary effects. Biochemical evaluation with plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines remains essential whenever PPGL is suspected, regardless of apparent alternative explanations ( 1 ).

Several limitations of this report should be acknowledged. As this is a single observational case, a causal relationship between cannabis use and the clinical expression of phaeochromocytoma cannot be established. Although the proposed CB1-mediated mechanism is biologically plausible, it was not directly demonstrated in this patient, and the temporal association between cannabis use and symptom variation may have been affected by other physiological or psychosocial factors. In addition, Ki-67, immunohistochemical profiling, and SDHB staining were not available, limiting the completeness of pathological risk assessment. Genetic counselling and germline testing were not performed, so an underlying hereditary predisposition cannot be excluded. These limitations reflect the nature of a single-case report and point to areas that warrant further investigation.

The increasing prevalence of cannabis use, with an estimated 219 million users globally, underscores the need to examine its potential health impacts. This review focuses on the arrhythmogenic properties of cannabis, particularly considering its active component, tetrahydrocannabinol, and its interactions with the endocannabinoid system. Epidemiological data and multiple studies indicate a significant association between cannabis use and various arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation. The risk is notably higher among younger users and males. Additionally, case reports have linked cannabis use to other arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, especially in individuals with underlying cardiac abnormalities. This review also discusses the arrhythmogenic potential of synthetic cannabinoids, which are more potent than natural tetrahydrocannabinol. Despite some studies suggesting no significant difference in arrhythmia burden between cannabis users and nonusers, the preponderance of evidence supports a correlation between cannabis use and increased arrhythmia risk. Given the rising tetrahydrocannabinol content in cannabis products and the limited data on the long-term cardiovascular effects, this review underscores the need for large-scale prospective studies. Until more comprehensive data are available, it is advisable for patients with channelopathies, structural heart disease, or prior myocardial infarction to avoid cannabis use.

Key Findings ▪ Cannabis use has been noted to have a temporal correlation with arrhythmias. ▪ Atrial fibrillation is the most common arrhythmia associated with cannabis use. ▪ Patients with channelopathies, structural heart disease, and prior myocardial infarction appear to have a significant association with cannabis induced arrhythmias. ▪ There is a paucity of large-scale prospective studies analyzing the correlation between cannabis use and arrhythmias. Until more data are available, it would be prudent to advise patients with the previously mentioned comorbidities to avoid marijuana use.

Introduction The global trend in drug use is on the rise, with an estimated 296 million users worldwide. Cannabis remains the most widely used drug, with approximately 219 million users in 2021, representing 4.3% of the global population 15 to 64 years of age. North America has the highest prevalence of cannabis use. Globally, about 70% of cannabis users are men, whereas in North America, 42% of users are women. According to the 2023 World Drug Report, the annual prevalence of cannabis use is disproportionately higher among adolescents (5.34% in 15–16 years of age) compared with adults (4.3%). 1

According to the data from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the top 5 commonly used drugs in the United States are cannabis (21.9% of the population), amphetamines (5.65%), nonmedical use of prescription opioids (3.9%), cocaine (2.4%), and nonmedical use of prescription stimulants (2.1%). 2 Several of these drugs exhibit arrhythmogenic potential. Additionally, co-use of marijuana and alcohol is highly prevalent in the United States, with about 58% of adolescent drinkers reporting marijuana use and over 75% of marijuana users reporting consuming alcohol. 3 Alcohol and marijuana together can intensify side effects of both, leading to increased cardiovascular risks due to synergistic effects. Sudden cardiac death from ingesting cannabis, along with alcohol has been reported. 4 However, the data on the arrhythmogenic potential of cannabis remain conflicting. This review aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the potential arrhythmogenic properties of cannabis based on available literature. “Cannabis” refers to all products (about 540 chemical substances) derived from the plant Cannabis sativa . “Marijuana” refers to parts or products containing significant amounts of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) from the plants Cannabis sativa or Cannabis indica . Cannabinoids are a group of substances found in the cannabis plant, mainly THC and cannabidiol (CBD). 5

As of August 8, 2024, cannabis has been legalized in 24 states for recreational use, along with Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands, and Washington, DC. 6 Despite its legalization in these regions, it remains classified as a Schedule I drug by the Drug Enforcement Administration, indicating drugs with no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for dependence and abuse. 7 , 8 The research reported in this paper adhered to the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines.

Pathophysiological effects of cannabis with an emphasis on arrhythmogenesis The electrophysiological effect of cannabis is multifaceted ( Figure 1 ). Cannabis primarily exerts its effects via the endocannabinoid system, involving G protein–coupled cannabinoid receptors, CB1 and CB2. THC is a partial agonist of CB1 and CB2 receptors. Activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors inhibit the enzyme adenylyl cyclase, leading to a reduction in cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels, resulting in inhibition of voltage-sensitive calcium channels (N-type, P/Q-type, and L-type) and D-type outward potassium channels, while G protein–activated inwardly rectifying potassium channels are activated. 9 These alterations can potentially disturb the electrical conduction system of the heart, increasing the risk of arrhythmias. CB1 receptor mediates an increase in heart rate and favors a shift toward increased sympathetic activity, resulting in enhanced sinus node automaticity. 10 Figure 1 Pathophysiology of arrhythmia with cannabis use.

Tachycardia may also result from THC induced parasympathetic vasodilatation. 11 Studies have shown increased plasma norepinephrine levels and increased urinary excretion of epinephrine following THC use. 12 Cannabis-induced adrenergic excitation has the potential to provoke tachyarrhythmia in predisposed individuals due to shortening of the action potential duration coupled with disturbances in the myocardial electrophysiology, which leads to automaticity and micro–re-entrant circuits. 13 In fact, THC induces a biphasic response with increased sympathetic activation and tachycardia at lower doses and bradycardia at higher doses. 14 The possible explanation of bradycardia/bradyarrhythmia is alteration of autonomic nervous system with reduction in sympathetic stimulation while there is enhanced parasympathetic reaction. 13

Medical cannabis products include dronabinol and CBD. Dronabinol is biochemically identical to THC and the arrhythmogenic pathophysiology is similar as described previously. CBD has a weak affinity for CB1 and CB2 receptors and does not possess the typical intoxicating/psychoactive properties associated with marijuana use. 15 , 16 CBD has purported anti-inflammatory and analgesic activities by cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase inhibition. 17 In an in vitro study on rabbit hearts, CBD was found to inhibit the Na v 1.5 sodium current, Ca v 1.2-mediated L-type calcium current, and all the repolarizing potassium currents except the delayed rectified current (K ir 2.1). No effects on resting membrane potential were observed due to the absence of effects on the K ir 2.1 current, except at rapid pacing rates. 18 CBD also leads to the inhibition of hERG/Ikr channel and QT prolongation. 19 Thus, CBD impacts cardiac ion channels, potentially leading to proarrhythmogenic effects, particularly in patients with cardiac channelopathies or in combination with other drugs affecting cardiac electrophysiological substrate.

Patients with channelopathies, structural heart disease, and prior myocardial infarction appear to have a significant association with marijuana-induced arrhythmias. Cannabinoids also affect key classes of antiarrhythmic medications through its inhibition of CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. This can cause elevated levels of antiarrhythmic drugs such as amiodarone, quinidine, lidocaine, mexiletine, flecainide, propafenone, and beta-blockers. However, data regarding dose adjustment are currently limited. 20

Synthetic cannabinoids are widely available and marketed under various names such as Spice, K2, Cloud 9, Black Mamba, etc. They are structurally classified into 7 groups (naphthoylindoles, naphthylmethylindoles, naphthoylpyrroles, naphthylmethylindenes, phenylacetylindoles, cyclohexylphenois, and classical cannabinoids). 21 Synthetic cannabinoids mimic the effects of THC on the cannabinoid receptor with greater binding affinity to the CB1 receptors and are multiple times more potent. Synthetic cannabinoids are full agonists of the CB1 receptor in contrast to natural THC, which is a partial agonist. 22 They mediate arrhythmias via receptor activation as well as interaction with myocardial ion channels. They also increase oxidative stress and cell death by interfering with the mitochondrial transport. 23

Arrhythmia burden with cannabis use The route of administration may influence the cardiovascular effects of cannabinoids. Oral administration results in slower absorption and more prolonged effects, whereas inhalation leads to rapid onset but shorter duration of action. Peak plasma concentration and the resultant cardiovascular effects, including arrhythmias, might be higher with inhaled forms compared with oral administration. 24 , 25 No study comparing the different forms of administration of cannabis was found on detailed literature search, and further study is needed.

There are multiple studies utilizing the National Inpatient Sample Database between 2010 and 2018 have investigated the association between marijuana use and arrhythmias. The reported incidence of arrhythmias in these studies has been up to 3% with the predominant arrhythmia being atrial fibrillation (AF). There appears to be a 47% to 52% increased likelihood of arrhythmia-related hospitalization in younger populations (15–34 years of age) with cannabis use. 26 , 27 Notably, there has been a male preponderant increase in arrhythmia-related hospitalizations among individuals with cannabis use, and is associated with worse in-hospital mortality outcomes and longer hospital stays. 28 , 29 In a Danish nationwide registry-based study, new-onset arrhythmias were observed more frequently among patients newly initiated on medical cannabis, with a relative risk increase of 64% compared with matched control subjects without prior arrhythmias. 30

Sinus tachycardia Studies examining drivers under the influence of cannabis have demonstrated higher mean pulse rates and increased incidence of sinus tachycardia (19.4% vs 1.6%). This was confirmed by delta-9-THC testing and positive status. There was no correlation between blood delta-9-THC concentration and pulse rate. 31 Several randomized controlled trials and experimental studies have consistently shown a dose-dependent increase in heart rate associated with marijuana use. Oral THC, smoked marijuana, and synthetic nabilone have all been implicated in elevating heart rate, suggesting a uniform physiological response across different modes of cannabis consumption. 32

Atrial fibrillation Database analyses, retrospective analyses, review articles, case series, and case reports have all suggested an association between marijuana use and AF. In 2 National Inpatient Sample Database studies, the most common arrhythmia associated with marijuana use was AF, with an estimated 42% of marijuana-related arrhythmias being attributed to AF. 26 , 27

Multiple case reports and case series suggest marijuana as a potential trigger for paroxysmal AF. 33 , 34 , 35 A review between the association of marijuana and AF by Korantzopoulos and colleagues 36 showed 6 patients with AF within minutes to 3 hours of use of marijuana. These patients had no structural heart disease, and were relatively young, with a mean age of 24.5 ± 7.8 years. The hypothesis was based on altered electrophysiologic properties of the myocardium favoring automaticity and micro–re-entry from adrenergic stimulation. In addition, coronary microcirculation–mediated atrial ischemia was also suggested as a potential etiopathogenic mechanism. 36 A retrospective study showed that 3.4% of lone AF in patients <45 years of age was precipitated by marijuana. 37

Supraventricular tachycardia The data on the association of marijuana with supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is limited. A cross-sectional analysis among 1485 participants from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) study with extended ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring with the Zio Patch XT (iRhythm) showed trends to more SVT per day (although not statistically significant). Additionally, there was an increase in premature atrial contractions and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), although it did not meet statistical significance. This was more prominent among current marijuana smokers in comparison with past users. 38

There have also been multiple case reports of SVT with marijuana use in patients with no prior cardiac history, and there are reports of successful SVT treatment with either cessation of cannabis use and beta-blockers alone. 11 , 38 , 39 Another interesting phenomenon is the possible interaction between marijuana and amitriptyline at the cytochrome level. A 17-year-old male on amitriptyline presented with a “racing heart” and was found to have SVT at a rate of 300 beats/min after consuming marijuana 12 hours prior. Screening was negative for other drugs. 40

Cannabis may also trigger atrioventricular tachycardia by enhancing accessory pathway conduction potentially via modulation of the autonomic nervous system. 41 Sudden cardiac arrest/VT/ventricular fibrillation The data on the correlation between malignant ventricular arrhythmias and marijuana use is largely limited to case reports and series ( Table 1 ). In patients with underlying structural heart disease and channelopathies, marijuana may trigger life-threatening arrhythmias. A 22-year-old African American male developed VT and torsades de pointes in the setting of marijuana use and subsequently found to have Brugada syndrome on his electrocardiogram. 43 The marijuana was believed to have triggered the arrhythmia in this case. A 60-year-old male with prior severe 3-vessel coronary artery disease and ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in situ had episodes of ventricular fibrillation (VF) that appeared to be triggered with high doses of marijuana use. 44

Case series have also shown an association between acute coronary syndromes with sudden cardiac arrest (including asystole, VT, and VF) in the absence of other risk factors besides recent marijuana use. 45 Several reported case fatalities related to use of marijuana appear to stem from its propensity to trigger myocardial infarction. Although there are many case reports of the same, there have been no epidemiological studies proving the association. Based on prior data, the risk of myocardial infarction is elevated 4.8 times over baseline in the hour after smoking cannabis and subsequently declines rapidly. 49 Marijuana use may trigger coronary slow flow with associated VT, which was reproducible on electrophysiologic testing. This resolved with verapamil therapy and cessation of marijuana use. A proposed theory was abnormalities of coronary microcirculation. 50

A case series by Hartung and colleagues 46 reported 2 cases of young males (23 and 28 years old, respectively) with death secondary to VF-mediated sudden cardiac arrest. Autopsy and toxicologic evaluations showed elevated cannabis levels in blood (THC: 1.9–5.2 ng/mL) with negative screening for other drugs. Cardiac arrest and death were suspected to be secondary to acute global cardiac failure under the influence of cannabis. 46 There have also been multiple cases suggestive of sudden cardiac arrest triggered by polysubstance use (cannabis in addition to cocaine/alcohol). 47

A review by Drummer and Gerostamoulos 48 provides a summary of 13 case fatalities related to marijuana use. All patients were male and 17 to 52 (median 37) years of age. Autopsy studies showed a spectrum from left ventricular mural thrombus with myocardial infarction, thrombi in the coronaries, dilated cardiomyopathy, vasospasm, and overt coronary artery disease. Arrhythmias ranged from asystole to VF. Twelve of these patients had a positive screening test for cannabis ( Table 1 ). 48

Bradyarrhythmias There have been numerous case reports on the association between marijuana use and bradyarrhythmia. The effects of marijuana in precipitating bradyarrhythmia vary from sinus node dysfunction to high-grade atrioventricular block. These effects may be mediated by high vagal tone and parasympathetic dominance, by tropism for adenosine receptors, or via direct effects on the myocardium by unidentified endothelial and cardiac receptors. 51

Acute cannabis smoking of low to moderate doses causes tachycardia in the first 60 minutes from sympathetic stimulation and parasympathetic inhibition, while large and/or chronic doses cause parasympathetic dominance that predisposes to bradycardias. 9 A study on prolonged THC ingestions in human volunteers and animals showed parasympathetic dominance featuring sinus bradycardia. There was also dose-dependent incidence of sinus arrest/asystole with long-term inhalation. 52 Studies have also shown that the bradycardic effects of THC were completely abolished in animals in which the autonomic pathways to the heart were pharmacologically or surgically inactivated suggesting an autonomic etiology for bradycardia. 53

An electrophysiology study performed in a 26-year-old male with chronic cannabis use who presented with atrioventricular block showed high-grade supra-Hisian (nodal) atrioventricular block with an AH interval of 180 ms and a prolonged HV interval of 85 ms. The electrophysiologic effects of THC on cardiac conduction include a change in P-wave morphology, decrease in SA conduction, delay in AH interval, and decrease in atrioventricular node refractory period. 54

Exercise-related asystole with syncope is rare in patients with structural heart disease. Presence of the same in the absence of structural heart disease portends an ominous sign. A 40-year-old healthy man was hospitalized with recurrent near syncope and an isolated syncopal episode after strenuous exercise while using marijuana. A monitored exercise test showed a loss of sinoatrial activity and ventricular asystole suggestive of parasympathetic dominance, potentially related to long-term cannabinoid use. 55

Synthetic cannabinoids The most common presentation with synthetic cannabinoid use is sinus tachycardia in young males (37%–77%). This has been demonstrated in multiple case reports and case series with sinus rates up to 220 beats/min. 22 , 56 , 57 , 58 SVT has been noted in case reports with synthetic cannabinoid ingestion. This is postulated to be secondary to increased circulating catecholamines or oxidative demands on the myocardium with CB1 receptor agonism. 59 , 60 In patients with supraventricular arrhythmias, chronic synthetic cannabinoid users had an increase in the dispersion values of P waves, which could indicate an early step in the genesis of AF. 23 There have also been reported cases of resistant VF and cardiogenic shock after synthetic cannabinoid use in young males. 61 They also pose the problem of often being undetectable on routine drug screens and are relatively low priced in comparison with traditional marijuana. 21

Medical cannabis Medical cannabis has been increasingly utilized for its analgesic, antiemetic, and anti-inflammatory properties. Compounds such as dronabinol (a synthetic form of THC), CBD, and nabilone (a synthetic cannabinoid) are commonly prescribed. A comprehensive literature search on PubMed using keywords "marijuana," "cannabis," "dronabinol," "cannabidiol," "CBD," "nabilone," "arrhythmia," and "cardiac arrhythmia" reported few studies linking medical cannabis use and arrhythmia. 62

CBD is approved by the Food and Drug Administration as an oral solution for treatment of intractable seizures (in >1 year of age), especially in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, and Dravet syndrome, with improved quality of life due to reduced frequency and intensity of seizures. 63 Dronabinol is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for treatment of anorexia in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. 64 Dronabinol and nabilone are suggested by the American Society of Clinical Oncology Focused Guideline for intractable chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in cancer patients. 65 , 66 , 67 Off-label, THC has been demonstrated to reduce intraocular pressure in patients with glaucoma, improvement in chronic pain and muscle spasms in patients with multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injuries, and improved neuropathic pain in patients with neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease and Tourette syndrome. 68 , 69 However, there still exists controversy and lack of enough randomized control trials to support these off-label uses.

Medical cannabis usually contains CBD unlike the recreational marijuana that has higher levels of THC. Additionally, medical use of cannabis is regulated with timely dosing and monitoring by the prescribing physician with the intention to reduce side effects. 70 Despite this, a recent nationwide Danish study showed that there was an elevated risk of new-onset arrhythmia associated with medical cannabis products containing THC or CBD for chronic pain. The largest risk difference was in patients with cancer or cardiometabolic disease with >75% of arrhythmia burden due to AF. The standardized 180-day risk ratio was 2.07. 71 There have also been reports of dose-dependent heart rate increase with oral dronabinol and nabilone. 62

In summary, patients who use recreational marijuana are at higher risk for overdose and arrhythmias because of lack of medical supervision and monitoring. Recreational use is episodic and could involve larger doses with associated greater propensity for arrhythmias.

Studies showing no correlation between cannabis and arrhythmias There appear to be fewer studies noting lack of correlation between cannabis and arrhythmias, and these are worth looking into. A prospective study comparing cannabis user healthy control subjects, cannabis user ischemic heart disease patients, and non–cannabis user ischemic heart disease patients showed no difference in overall arrhythmia burden. 72 However, this study did not compare healthy control subjects with and without cannabis use.

An outcome analysis on patients hospitalized with acute myocardial infarction and marijuana use showed that the marijuana cohort had less coronary artery disease and AF than nonusers. However, the marijuana cohort was younger by 10 years, raising the possibility of age being a confounder. Additionally, marijuana users tended to need hospitalization for acute myocardial infarction at younger ages. 73 A retrospective study showed less odds of AF in patients with admitted with heart failure among cannabis users. No measure of temporal correlation between cannabis use and AF was provided. 74

CBD has been suggested to have some protective effects against high glucose-induced oxidative stress and cytotoxicity in cardiac voltage-gated sodium channels. This has been postulated to provide an antiarrhythmic effect. 75 However, there has been a decline in CBD content with rising trend in THC content in most seized marijuana in the United States, with a current THC content of about 50%. This increasing THC content can be inherently more harmful, as we have discussed previously. 76

Screening for cannabis use We advocate for routine screening for cannabis use including frequency, quantity, and methods of administration in the social history. Marijuana testing is currently required prior to an evaluation for heart transplantation. It may be reasonable to perform urine toxicology in the setting of myocardial infarction and new-onset heart failure. 20 In a clinical framework, the detection of cannabis is predominantly performed via urine analysis, in which its principal component, delta-9-THC, or its metabolite 11-hydroxy-delta-9-THC is identified. 77 , 78 Although it is possible to detect cannabis through blood, hair, or saliva, these methods are not typically implemented in routine clinical practice. 79 , 80 , 81 Postingestion, cannabis can be traced in plasma almost immediately, with blood sample measurements offering a more accurate reflection of the individual’s level of exposure, as the concentrations of the drug in urine can fluctuate due to metabolic variations and urine production. 78 Due to their lipophilic nature, most cannabinoids have long elimination half-life. 82 Approximately 80%–90% of delta-9-THC is expelled from the body within 5 days but may be detectable for up to 2 weeks in occasional users, and even longer in chronic users. 78 Immunoassay is the routine testing method but analytical methods like gas chromatography mass spectrometry or liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry can be used for accurate quantification. 83 , 84 , 85

Nonprescription synthetic cannabinoids have a high potential for pharmacologic manipulation and increased potency. Additionally, synthetic cannabinoids do not show up in a routine urine drug screen, as they are not structurally similar to THC. In terms of synthetic cannabinoids, their metabolites are the target of detection. The Synthetic Drug Abuse Prevention Act of 2021 listed the synthetic metabolites of interest, which may be detected more in blood, hair, or saliva. 86 , 87 The biggest challenge is the emergence of newer compounds with unknown metabolites making detection harder. There are no available data on lab testing of medical marijuana, and this is an area that needs further research.

Conclusion Cannabinoids appear to have a temporal correlation with arrhythmias which subside with prolonged periods of abstinence. While studies have suggested that frequency of marijuana use may correlate with more ectopy, data on a possible safe dose of marijuana are lacking. 20 In addition, there is a significantly higher preponderance in younger males to adverse effects of marijuana, which is likely secondary to the highest use, and possibly in higher doses in the corresponding demographic. Patients should be counseled regarding concurrent use of other illicit drugs. It is important to discuss with the patients not only the limited scientific data at hand, but also the possible association of marijuana and arrhythmias, especially in higher-risk groups. 20

While medical marijuana may offer significant therapeutic benefits, the potential for arrhythmias should always be considered. Therefore, healthcare providers must weigh the benefits against the risks, especially in patients with pre-existing heart conditions. Close monitoring and individualized treatment plans are essential to minimize the risk of adverse cardiac events. Further research is needed to establish clear guidelines and ensure the safe use of medical marijuana. The method of administration is particularly important, with inhaled forms likely to pose a higher risk for arrhythmias compared with oral forms, though no formal study was found in this area.

We highlight the paucity of large-scale prospective studies analyzing the correlation between marijuana and arrhythmias. With the advent of consumer wearable health technology and long-term electrocardiographic monitoring, this would likely be a more feasible option in the future. Until we have large-scale data, it would be prudent to advise patients with the previously mentioned comorbidities to avoid marijuana use.

Introduction Energy drinks are widely marketed to enhance alertness and performance, making them a rapidly growing industry valued at $73.99 billion. These beverages typically contain caffeine and other stimulants, but their consumption has raised concerns about potential cardiovascular risks, including arrhythmias, tachycardia, and hypertension, particularly among young adults. While moderate caffeine intake may offer health benefits, excessive consumption of energy drinks has been linked to increased cardiovascular risks. This systematic review aims to explore the cardiovascular effects of energy drink consumption, identify knowledge gaps, and guide clinicians in making recommendations.

Methods A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, CINAHL, MEDLINE, PubMed, and others. Studies were screened for those involving energy drink consumption and cardiovascular outcomes such as heart rate, blood pressure, and ECG changes. After screening abstracts, full-text articles were reviewed based on inclusion criteria: participants aged 13+, energy drink consumption, and relevant cardiovascular endpoints.

Results A total of 1,444 references were screened, resulting in 37 studies with 1,597 participants (mean age 22.6). Red Bull and Monster were the most studied brands. Results showed significant cardiovascular effects, including increased heart rate (60.9%), systolic blood pressure (53.8%), diastolic blood pressure (61.5%), and QTc interval prolongation (63.2%). Other ECG changes, such as PR interval and T-wave alterations, were observed in 57.9% of studies. Conclusion This review highlights the cardiovascular risks of energy drinks, including increased heart rate, blood pressure, and QTc prolongation. Future research should focus on at-risk groups and long-term effects.
